title: Spread the letter (2 Kings 19:14–19)
hookLine: King Hezekiah spreads the threatening letter before God
carry: lay it open before you answer
tomorrow: I have seen thy tears (2 Kings 20:1–6)

cards: A letter arrives, and it isn't the first message. Assyria's officer has already stood outside the walls of Jerusalem and shouted, in Hebrew so everyone on the wall could understand: don't let your king fool you.
No god of any nation has saved its land from us. Now the king of Assyria, Sennacherib, puts it in writing and sends it to King Hezekiah. Every word is built to make him give up.
And Hezekiah does not answer it the way it asks to be answered.

teach.b: The text says Hezekiah received the letter from the messengers and read it.
Then he went up to the house of the Lord, "and spread it before the LORD." He doesn't answer it, or tear it up, or hide it in a drawer and lie awake.
He walks it into the Temple and unrolls it, as if to say: here, read this with me. Then he prays, and the prayer has a shape. It doesn't start with the threat.

It starts with who God is: the God of all the kingdoms of the earth, who made heaven and earth. Only then does he ask: incline your ear and hear, open your eyes and see these words, sent to mock the living God.
Next, Hezekiah tells the truth about the danger.

Yes, the kings of Assyria really have laid waste nations and their lands, and thrown their gods into the fire, because those were no gods, only wood and stone made by human hands. He names it plainly.
And then the ask: save us out of his hand, so that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that you alone are God.

teach.h: WHO GOD IS, WHAT'S TRUE, WHAT WE NEED.
teach.b: Who God is, what's true, what we need. The letter didn't change. The army didn't move.

But the king is no longer holding the threat alone in his fist. It's laid open in the house of the Lord, a picture of prayer as a page laid out, with nothing hidden. What happens next belongs to another day.

how: Jews read Hezekiah's prayer as part of the book of Kings, and the same story is told again in Isaiah 37; some readers take it as a picture of honest prayer in danger.

games.q: you're the king. an enemy's letter says no god can save you. what do you do with it?
o: take it to the Temple and spread it before God.
burn it and tell no one.
games.why: Hezekiah reads it, goes up to the house of the Lord and spreads it out there, then prays.

practice: Pick one worry, the one that's been arriving like a letter all week, and in your mind unroll it and lay it flat on a table, so you can see the whole thing.
Read it honestly, without arguing: what's true here, and what's only threat? Then leave it there, open, and let your hands rest; if you pray, you can spread it before God, as Hezekiah did.

wordCard.voice: Hezekiah, who carried Sennacherib's threatening letter into the Temple and spread it open before God instead of holding it alone.

orig.note: Hebrew: to spread out, the verb used for what Hezekiah did with the letter.

carryVoice: Your line: lay it open before you answer. The danger can be real and still not held alone. Day seven hundred seventy-eight, done.
